# Time & Work

## Concepts

### Work, workers and time

For equally efficient workers working at a constant rate, the amount of work completed is proportional to the number of workers and the time spent working. For a fixed job, workers and time are inversely proportional.

> [!abstract] Core idea
> For a fixed job with equally efficient workers, **workers × days = constant**.

## Formulas / rules

### Constant work

If work and efficiency per worker remain unchanged:

$$
W_1D_1=W_2D_2
$$

where W is the number of workers and D is the number of days.

The total work can be measured in worker-days:

$$
\text{Total work}=\text{Workers}\times\text{Days}
$$

This assumes equal efficiency, equal daily working hours and unchanged working conditions.

## Worked examples

### Trick 2. Constant work — changing the number of workers

**Question**

Suppose 10 workers finish a job in 12 days. How many days will 15 equally efficient workers take?

**Traditional method**

Total work:

$$
10\times12=120\text{ worker-days}
$$

Let the new time be T:

$$
15T=120
$$

$$
T=8\text{ days}
$$

> [!success] Answer
> **8 days.**

**Shortcut**

$$
W_1D_1=W_2D_2
$$

$$
10\times12=15\times T
$$

$$
T=\frac{120}{15}=8\text{ days}
$$

> [!tip] CAT shortcut
> When equally efficient workers increase in number, the time decreases inversely. Cross-multiply directly.

## Common traps

- Do not apply the inverse-proportion shortcut blindly when workers have different efficiencies.
- The total job must remain unchanged.
- Daily working hours and individual productivity must remain constant.

## Practice and mistakes

- [ ] I can calculate total work in worker-days.
- [ ] I can apply W₁D₁ = W₂D₂ to a fixed job.
- [ ] I check the equal-efficiency assumption.

# Time, Speed & Distance

## Concepts

### Relationship between speed, distance and time

$$
S=\frac{D}{T}
$$

For a fixed distance, speed and time are inversely proportional. If speed increases, the time required to cover the same distance decreases.

> [!abstract] Core idea
> For a fixed distance, **speed × time = constant**.

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 5bfa2d5c45fe7e46 -->
### Average speed

Average speed is always total distance divided by total time:

$$
\boxed{\text{Average speed}=\frac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Total time}}}
$$

It is not automatically the arithmetic mean of the speeds. The correct shortcut depends on whether the journey has equal distances or equal times.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 5bfa2d5c45fe7e46 -->

## Formulas / rules

### Constant distance

When distance remains unchanged:

$$
S_1T_1=S_2T_2
$$

If speed increases by x%, its multiplier is 1 + x/100. The time multiplier is the reciprocal:

$$
\frac{1}{1+x/100}
$$

The percentage decrease in time is:

$$
\frac{x}{100+x}\times100
$$

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 7a296d64d0c9f5f3 -->
### Average-speed shortcuts

**Two equal-distance journeys**

For two equal-distance journeys at speeds u and v:

$$
\boxed{\text{Average speed}=\frac{2uv}{u+v}}
$$

This is the harmonic mean.

**Two equal-time journeys**

If a vehicle travels for equal amounts of time at speeds u and v:

$$
\boxed{\text{Average speed}=\frac{u+v}{2}}
$$

This is the arithmetic mean.

**Decision rule:** Equal distances → harmonic mean. Equal times → arithmetic mean. If neither is equal, calculate total distance ÷ total time directly.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 7a296d64d0c9f5f3 -->

## Worked examples

### Trick 3. Constant distance — speed increases by 20%

**Question**

A car travels a fixed distance. Its speed increases by 20%. Find the percentage decrease in time.

**Traditional method**

Assume distance = 120 km and original speed = 60 km/h.

Original time:

$$
T_1=\frac{120}{60}=2\text{ hours}
$$

New speed:

$$
60\times1.20=72\text{ km/h}
$$

New time:

$$
T_2=\frac{120}{72}=\frac{5}{3}\text{ hours}
$$

Percentage decrease:

$$
\frac{2-5/3}{2}\times100=16.67\%
$$

> [!success] Answer
> **16.67% decrease in time (approximately).**

**Shortcut**

$$
S_1T_1=S_2T_2
$$

A 20% speed increase makes speed 120% of its original value. Therefore, time becomes 100/120 = 5/6 of its original value.

$$
\left(1-\frac{5}{6}\right)\times100=16.67\%
$$

> [!tip] CAT shortcut
> A 20% increase in speed does not cause a 20% decrease in time. Use the reciprocal factor.

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: beecf83aa0758656 -->
### Example — Equal distances

A car travels 60 km at 30 km/h and another 60 km at 60 km/h.

Times:

$$
t_1=\frac{60}{30}=2\text{ h},\qquad t_2=\frac{60}{60}=1\text{ h}
$$

Average speed:

$$
\frac{120}{2+1}=\boxed{40\text{ km/h}}
$$

**Shortcut — harmonic mean**

$$
\frac{2\times30\times60}{30+60}=\boxed{40\text{ km/h}}
$$

### Question 25 — Unequal distances, equal times

**Question:** A car travels 40 km at 40 km/h and another 80 km at 80 km/h. Find its average speed.

**Step 1: Calculate each time**

$$
t_1=\frac{40}{40}=1\text{ hour}
$$

$$
t_2=\frac{80}{80}=1\text{ hour}
$$

**Step 2: Total distance and time**

$$
D=40+80=120\text{ km},\qquad T=1+1=2\text{ hours}
$$

**Step 3: Average speed**

$$
\frac{120}{2}=\boxed{60\text{ km/h}}
$$

**Shortcut:** The durations are equal, so use the arithmetic mean:

$$
\frac{40+80}{2}=\boxed{60\text{ km/h}}
$$

**Trap:** The distances are unequal, so do not use the equal-distance harmonic-mean formula.

### Question 30 — Equal halves of a journey

**Question:** A person travels half of a journey at 30 km/h and the other half at 60 km/h. Find the average speed for the entire journey.

**Step 1: Identify the condition**

The distances are equal, not the times. Use the harmonic mean.

**Step 2: Apply the shortcut**

$$
\text{Average speed}=\frac{2uv}{u+v}
$$

$$
=\frac{2\times30\times60}{30+60}=\boxed{40\text{ km/h}}
$$

**Traditional verification:** Assume the total journey is 120 km, so each half is 60 km.

$$
t_1=\frac{60}{30}=2\text{ hours},\qquad
t_2=\frac{60}{60}=1\text{ hour}
$$

$$
\text{Average speed}=\frac{120}{2+1}=\boxed{40\text{ km/h}}
$$

**Answer: 40 km/h.**

**Trap:** Do not use (30 + 60)/2 = 45 km/h. The arithmetic mean applies to equal-time travel, not equal-distance travel.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: beecf83aa0758656 -->

## Common traps

- The inverse relationship applies only when distance is fixed.
- Do not equate the percentage increase in speed with the percentage decrease in time.
- Keep units consistent in S = D/T.

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: e6fe475946f50ee0 -->
### Average-speed traps

- **Always start with total distance ÷ total time.**
- Equal distances call for the harmonic mean, not the arithmetic mean.
- Equal times call for the arithmetic mean.
- If neither distance nor time is equal, calculate each leg's time and use total distance ÷ total time.
- Do not assume a 20% increase in speed creates a 20% decrease in time; for fixed distance, use reciprocal multipliers.
- Keep distance, time and speed units consistent.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: e6fe475946f50ee0 -->

## Practice and mistakes

- [ ] I can identify when distance is constant.
- [ ] I can use S₁T₁ = S₂T₂.
- [ ] I calculate percentage change using the original time as the base.

# Successive Percentage Change

> [!abstract] Core idea
> For successive percentage changes, **convert each change into a multiplier and multiply the multipliers**. Do not simply add or subtract the percentages.

## 1. The multiplier method

| Change | Multiply by |
|---|---:|
| Increase by 10% | **1.10** |
| Increase by 20% | **1.20** |
| Decrease by 10% | **0.90** |
| Decrease by 25% | **0.75** |

**General rule**

- Increase by r%: multiplier = **1 + r/100**
- Decrease by r%: multiplier = **1 − r/100**

Multiply all the multipliers to get the final value as a fraction of the original.

## 2. Worked example

**Question:** A town's population increases by 10% in the first year, increases by 20% in the second year, and decreases by 25% in the third year. Find the overall percentage change.

> [!tip] Choose a convenient starting value
> Assume the initial population is **1,000**. This makes the arithmetic straightforward.

| Stage | Calculation | Population |
|---|---:|---:|
| Initial | — | **1,000** |
| Year 1: +10% | 1,000 × 1.10 | 1,100 |
| Year 2: +20% | 1,100 × 1.20 | 1,320 |
| Year 3: −25% | 1,320 × 0.75 | **990** |

**Find the net percentage change**

$$
\text{Percentage change}
=\frac{\text{Final}-\text{Initial}}{\text{Initial}}\times100
$$

$$
=\frac{990-1000}{1000}\times100=-1\%
$$

> [!success] Answer
> **1% decrease.**

### Shortcut: Multiply the factors

$$
1.10\times1.20\times0.75=0.99
$$

The final population is **99%** of the original.

$$
(0.99-1)\times100=-1\%
$$

**Answer: 1% decrease.**

## 3. Why adding the percentages is wrong

A common mistake is:

$$
10\%+20\%-25\%=5\%
$$

This is incorrect because every change is applied to the **updated value**, not always to the original value.

- Year 1's 10% is applied to 1,000.
- Year 2's 20% is applied to 1,100.
- Year 3's 25% decrease is applied to 1,320.

The multiplier method automatically handles these changing bases.

## 4. CAT shortcut: Same increase and decrease

If a value increases by x% and then decreases by x%, the changes do **not** cancel.

$$
\text{Net decrease}=\frac{x^2}{100}\%
$$

**Example: +20%, then −20%**

$$
1.20\times0.80=0.96
$$

The final value is **96%** of the original.

> [!important] Result
> **Net change: 4% decrease.**

## 5. General formula

For successive changes of a%, b%, c%, use positive values for increases and negative values for decreases.

$$
\text{Final value}
=\text{Initial value}
\left(1+\frac{a}{100}\right)
\left(1+\frac{b}{100}\right)
\left(1+\frac{c}{100}\right)
$$

$$
\boxed{
\text{Overall change (\%)}
=
\left[
\left(1+\frac{a}{100}\right)
\left(1+\frac{b}{100}\right)
\left(1+\frac{c}{100}\right)-1
\right]\times100
}
$$

- Product greater than 1 → overall increase.
- Product less than 1 → overall decrease.
- Product equal to 1 → no change.

## 6. Timed CAT-style practice

*These are original practice questions, not claimed previous-year CAT questions.*

### Q1. Reverse an increase

A number is increased by 40%. By what percentage must the increased number be decreased to return to the original number?

<small>Suggested time: 60 seconds</small>

**Solution**

Assume the original number is 100.

$$
100\times1.40=140
$$

Required decrease = 140 − 100 = **40**.

The decrease percentage is calculated on 140:

$$
\frac{40}{140}\times100
=\frac{2}{7}\times100
\approx28.57\%
$$

> [!success] Answer
> **28.57% decrease (approximately).**

> [!warning] CAT trap
> To reverse a 40% increase, do not decrease by 40%. The base is now 140, not 100.

### Q2. Equal increase and decrease

A quantity increases by 25% and then decreases by 25%. Find the overall percentage change.

**Solution**

$$
1.25\times0.75=0.9375
$$

The final value is **93.75%** of the original.

> [!success] Answer
> **6.25% decrease.**

### Q3. Two successive increases

The price of an item increases by 10% in one month and by 10% in the next month. Find the total percentage increase.

**Solution**

$$
1.10\times1.10=1.21
$$

The final price is **121%** of the original.

> [!success] Answer
> **21% increase.**

## 7. Quick revision

> [!summary] Remember this
> 1. Increase by r% → multiply by 1 + r/100.
> 2. Decrease by r% → multiply by 1 − r/100.
> 3. Multiply the factors in sequence.
> 4. Compare the final factor with 1 to find the net change.
>
> **Never add successive percentages blindly.**

## 8. Self-check

- [ ] I can convert an increase into a multiplier.
- [ ] I can convert a decrease into a multiplier.
- [ ] I know each change applies to the updated value.
- [ ] I can calculate the net percentage change.
- [ ] I can reverse a percentage increase correctly.

# Profit, Loss & Discount

## Concepts

### Cost price, selling price and marked price

- **Cost Price (CP):** Amount paid by the shopkeeper to acquire the item.
- **Selling Price (SP):** Amount at which the item is sold.
- **Marked Price (MP):** Displayed price before discount.
- **Profit:** SP − CP, when SP is greater than CP.
- **Discount:** MP − SP.

Profit percentage is calculated on cost price; discount percentage is calculated on marked price.

> [!abstract] Core idea
> Keep the reference bases separate: **profit % uses CP; discount % uses MP**.

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 0d9400a9daa026ec -->
### Trick: Same selling price, one profit and one loss

A shopkeeper sells two articles at the same selling price. On one article, the gain is x%; on the other, the loss is x%.

For equal selling prices and equal profit/loss percentages, the overall result is always a loss:

$$
\text{Overall loss}\%=\frac{x^2}{100}
$$

**Example: 20% gain and 20% loss**

$$
\text{Loss}\%=\frac{20^2}{100}=4\%
$$

The result is not zero because the two articles have different cost prices. The article sold at a loss has the higher cost price.

### Trick: False weights

A dishonest seller may charge for 1 kg but supply only 900 g, while claiming to sell at cost price.

Assume the cost of 1 kg is ₹100. The seller collects ₹100 but supplies goods costing only ₹90.

$$
\text{Profit}\%=\frac{100-90}{90}\times100=11.11\%
$$

**Shortcut:** When the seller charges for the stated quantity but supplies less, calculate profit using the cost of the actual quantity supplied as the denominator.

### Trick: Reverse calculations

If SP and profit percentage are known:

$$
CP=\frac{SP}{1+p/100}
$$

If SP and loss percentage are known:

$$
CP=\frac{SP}{1-l/100}
$$

If SP and discount percentage are known:

$$
MP=\frac{SP}{1-d/100}
$$

Here, p = profit percentage, l = loss percentage and d = discount percentage.

### Trick: Markup followed by discount

If MP is 40% above CP and a discount of 25% is offered:

$$
SP=CP\times1.4\times0.75
$$

$$
SP=1.05CP
$$

Therefore, profit = 5%.

**General shortcut:** Convert every percentage change into a multiplier and multiply the factors. Do not add successive percentage changes directly.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 0d9400a9daa026ec -->

## Formulas / rules

For a profit of p%:

$$
SP=CP\left(1+\frac{p}{100}\right)
$$

For a discount of d%:

$$
SP=MP\left(1-\frac{d}{100}\right)
$$

When both are given, equate the two expressions for SP:

$$
CP\left(1+\frac{p}{100}\right)=MP\left(1-\frac{d}{100}\right)
$$

Therefore:

$$
\frac{MP}{CP}=\frac{1+p/100}{1-d/100}
$$

## Worked examples

### Q17. Marked price above cost price

**Question**

A shopkeeper gives a discount of 25% on the marked price but still earns a profit of 20%. By what percentage is the marked price above the cost price?

**Concept being tested**

Discount is calculated on marked price, whereas profit is calculated on cost price. Convert both statements into selling-price relationships and equate them.

**Step-by-step solution**

Assume CP = 100.

A profit of 20% gives:

$$
SP=100\times1.20=120
$$

A discount of 25% means SP is 75% of MP:

$$
120=0.75MP
$$

$$
MP=\frac{120}{0.75}=160
$$

The marked price is 60 above the cost price of 100:

$$
\frac{160-100}{100}\times100=60\%
$$

> [!success] Final answer
> **The marked price is 60% above the cost price.**

> [!tip] CAT shortcut
> Since SP is 120% of CP and 75% of MP:

$$
\frac{MP}{CP}=\frac{120}{75}=1.6
$$

Thus MP is 160% of CP, i.e. 60% higher.

> [!warning] Common trap
> Do not subtract the 25% discount from the 20% profit. These percentages have different bases.

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 726c2035fb9c25c5 -->
### Example: Marked price and discount

An article is marked 60% above CP. A discount of 25% is offered. Find the profit percentage.

Assume CP = ₹100.

- MP = ₹160.
- SP = ₹160 × 0.75 = ₹120.
- Profit = ₹20.

Therefore, profit = 20%.

**Shortcut:**

$$
SP=CP\times1.6\times0.75=1.2CP
$$

### Example: Find the required discount

An article is marked 50% above CP. What discount should be offered to earn 20% profit?

Assume CP = ₹100.

- MP = ₹150.
- Required SP = ₹120.
- Discount amount = ₹30.

$$
\text{Discount}\%=\frac{30}{150}\times100=20\%
$$

**Answer: 20% discount.**

### Example: Two successive transactions

A person sells an article at 20% profit. The buyer resells it at a 10% loss. Find the final selling price as a percentage of the original CP.

Assume original CP = ₹100.

- First SP = ₹120.
- Second SP = ₹120 × 0.9 = ₹108.

$$
\text{Final SP}=100\times1.2\times0.9=108
$$

The final selling price is 108% of original CP. Overall increase = 8%.

### Example: Same SP, one profit and one loss

A shopkeeper sells two articles at the same selling price. On one he earns 20% profit and on the other he suffers 20% loss. Find the overall profit/loss.

Assume SP of each article = ₹120.

$$
CP_1=\frac{120}{1.2}=₹100
$$

$$
CP_2=\frac{120}{0.8}=₹150
$$

Total CP = ₹250; total SP = ₹240; loss = ₹10.

$$
\text{Loss}\%=\frac{10}{250}\times100=4\%
$$

**Shortcut:**

$$
\text{Loss}\%=\frac{20^2}{100}=4\%
$$

**Answer: 4% loss.**

### Example: Markup and discount

Suppose MP is 40% above CP and a discount of 25% is offered.

$$
SP=CP\times1.4\times0.75=1.05CP
$$

**Answer: 5% profit.**
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 726c2035fb9c25c5 -->

## Common traps

- Profit percentage is not calculated on selling price.
- Discount percentage is not calculated on cost price.
- A discount and a profit can coexist if the marked price is sufficiently above cost price.
- When percentages refer to different bases, use multipliers and equate the selling price.

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: ebf92a75e3ed80ad -->
### Common traps and quick checks

- **Same SP does not mean same CP.** For equal SP with equal gain/loss percentages, the loss-side article has the higher CP.
- **Do not cancel equal gain and loss percentages.** Equal SP with 20% gain and 20% loss gives 4% overall loss.
- **False-weight denominator:** Use the cost of the actual quantity supplied when calculating the dealer's real profit.
- **Discount is on MP; profit/loss is on CP.**
- **Successive discounts are multiplicative.** A 15% discount followed by 20% is 32%, not 35%.
- **Changed CP and SP:** If both change, express the new CP and SP relative to the original CP before forming the equation.
- **Weighted profit/loss:** Use weights proportional to CP contribution. If CP per unit is uniform, stock proportions can be used directly.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: ebf92a75e3ed80ad -->

## Practice and mistakes

- [ ] I can distinguish CP, SP and MP.
- [ ] I calculate profit percentage on CP.
- [ ] I calculate discount percentage on MP.
- [ ] I can equate two expressions for SP.

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 684ef58cf7b32232 -->
## Level 3 — Difficult CAT applications

### Q17. Successive discounts

A shopkeeper offers successive discounts of 20% and 10%. If the final selling price is ₹720, find MP.

**Solution — multiplier method**

After the two discounts, the customer pays 80% × 90% of MP.

$$
720=MP\times0.8\times0.9
$$

$$
MP=\frac{720}{0.72}=\boxed{₹1,000}
$$

**Shortcut — equivalent discount**

$$
D=20+10-\frac{20\times10}{100}=28\%
$$

SP is 72% of MP, so MP = ₹1,000.

**Answer: ₹1,000.**

### Q18. Difference in selling prices

An article is sold at 25% profit. If it had been sold for ₹100 more, profit would have been 35%. Find CP.

**Solution**

Let CP = x.

$$
1.35x-1.25x=100
$$

$$
0.10x=100\Rightarrow x=\boxed{₹1,000}
$$

**Shortcut:** The profit rate increases by 10 percentage points. That increase in SP is 10% of CP.

$$
CP=\frac{100\times100}{10}=₹1,000
$$

**Answer: ₹1,000.**

### Q19. CP and SP both reduced

A trader sells an article at 20% profit. If both CP and SP were ₹100 lower, the profit percentage would be 25%. Find original CP.

**Solution**

Let original CP = x. Original profit = 20% of x. Reducing both CP and SP by ₹100 leaves the absolute profit unchanged.

$$
0.2x=0.25(x-100)
$$

$$
0.2x=0.25x-25
$$

$$
0.05x=25\Rightarrow x=\boxed{₹500}
$$

**Shortcut:** Since the absolute profit remains the same, equate the original profit amount to 25% of the reduced CP.

**Answer: ₹500.**

### Q20. Markup followed by discount

A shopkeeper marks an article 80% above CP and offers a discount of 25%. What is the profit percentage?

**Solution**

Assume CP = ₹100.

- MP = ₹180.
- SP = ₹180 × 0.75 = ₹135.
- Profit = ₹35.

**Shortcut:**

$$
\frac{SP}{CP}=1.8\times0.75=1.35
$$

**Answer: 35% profit.**

### Q21. Same selling price, one gain and one loss

A trader sells two articles for ₹1,200 each. He gains 20% on the first and loses 20% on the second. Find his total loss.

**Solution**

$$
CP_1=\frac{1200}{1.2}=₹1,000
$$

$$
CP_2=\frac{1200}{0.8}=₹1,500
$$

Total CP = ₹2,500; total SP = ₹2,400. Loss = ₹100.

$$
\text{Loss}\%=\frac{100}{2500}\times100=4\%
$$

**Shortcut — equal SP and equal gain/loss rate:**

$$
\text{Loss}\%=\frac{20^2}{100}=4\%
$$

**Answer: ₹100 loss, or 4%.**

### Q22. Different quantities sold at different rates

A person purchases 100 articles for ₹80 each. He sells 60 articles at 25% profit and the remaining at 10% loss. Find total profit percentage.

**Solution**

Total CP = 100 × ₹80 = ₹8,000.

First 60 articles:

$$
CP_1=60\times80=₹4,800
$$

$$
SP_1=4800\times1.25=₹6,000
$$

Remaining 40 articles:

$$
CP_2=40\times80=₹3,200
$$

$$
SP_2=3200\times0.9=₹2,880
$$

Total SP = ₹8,880. Profit = ₹880.

$$
\text{Profit}\%=\frac{880}{8000}\times100=11\%
$$

**Shortcut — weighted average, since CP per article is uniform:**

$$
0.60(25\%)+0.40(-10\%)=15\%-4\%=11\%
$$

**Answer: 11% profit.**

### Q23. Equivalent single discount

A shopkeeper gives two successive discounts of 15% and 20%. Find the single equivalent discount.

**Solution**

$$
\text{Price factor}=0.85\times0.80=0.68
$$

The customer pays 68% of MP, so the discount is 32%.

**Shortcut:**

$$
D=15+20-\frac{15\times20}{100}=32\%
$$

**Answer: 32%.**

### Q24. Required markup after discount

A trader wants to earn 30% profit after offering a 20% discount. By what percentage should MP exceed CP?

**Solution**

Assume CP = ₹100. Required SP = ₹130.

$$
130=0.8MP
$$

$$
MP=\frac{130}{0.8}=₹162.50
$$

Markup = ₹62.50, so markup percentage = 62.5%.

**Shortcut:**

$$
\frac{MP}{CP}=\frac{1.30}{0.80}=1.625
$$

**Answer: 62.5% markup.**

## Level 4 — Challenge

### Q25. Dishonest dealer: loss on price, gain through short weight

A dishonest dealer sells goods at 10% loss but uses a weight that is 20% less than the stated weight. Find actual profit/loss percentage.

**Solution**

Assume the cost of 1 kg is ₹100.

At 10% loss on the stated 1 kg, the dealer collects:

$$
SP=100\times0.9=₹90
$$

But he supplies only 800 g. The actual cost of 800 g is:

$$
CP_{\text{actual}}=100\times0.8=₹80
$$

Actual profit = ₹90 − ₹80 = ₹10.

$$
\text{Actual profit}\%=\frac{10}{80}\times100=12.5\%
$$

**Shortcut — compare revenue with actual cost:**

$$
\frac{SP}{CP_{\text{actual}}}=\frac{0.9}{0.8}=1.125
$$

**Answer: 12.5% actual profit.**

**Trap:** The 10% loss is on the stated quantity's price. Actual cost is for the smaller quantity supplied.

### Q26. Changed CP and changed SP

A shopkeeper sells an article at 10% profit. If he had purchased it at 10% less and sold it for ₹20 less, his profit would have been 20%. Find original CP.

**Solution**

Let original CP = x. Original SP = 1.1x.

New CP = 0.9x. New SP = 1.1x − 20.

The new profit is 20% on the new CP:

$$
1.1x-20=1.2(0.9x)
$$

$$
1.1x-20=1.08x
$$

$$
0.02x=20\Rightarrow x=\boxed{₹1,000}
$$

**Shortcut — compare both SPs as percentages of original CP:**

New SP = 120% × 90% = 108% of original CP. Original SP = 110%. Difference = 2% of original CP = ₹20.

$$
CP=\frac{20\times100}{2}=₹1,000
$$

**Answer: ₹1,000.**

### Q27. Different portions of stock sold at different rates

A trader sells 40% of his stock at 20% profit, 30% at 10% loss and the remaining at 15% profit. Find overall profit percentage, assuming uniform CP per unit.

**Solution — weighted average**

$$
0.40(20\%)+0.30(-10\%)+0.30(15\%)
$$

$$
=8\%-3\%+4.5\%=9.5\%
$$

**Verification:** Assume total CP = ₹100.

| Portion | CP | Profit/loss | SP |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 40% | ₹40 | +₹8 | ₹48 |
| 30% | ₹30 | −₹3 | ₹27 |
| 30% | ₹30 | +₹4.50 | ₹34.50 |
| **Total** | **₹100** | **+₹9.50** | **₹109.50** |

**Answer: 9.5% profit.**

**Shortcut condition:** Weighted average by stock percentage is valid here because CP per unit is uniform.

### Q28. Discount offered but profit maintained

A trader offers 20% discount on MP and still earns 25% profit. Find markup percentage over CP.

**Solution**

Assume CP = ₹100. For 25% profit, SP = ₹125.

$$
125=0.8MP
$$

$$
MP=\frac{125}{0.8}=₹156.25
$$

Markup = ₹56.25, so markup percentage = 56.25%.

**Shortcut:**

$$
\frac{MP}{CP}=\frac{1.25}{0.8}=1.5625
$$

**Answer: 56.25% markup.**

### Q29. Changed CP and SP with a new profit rate

A shopkeeper sells an article at 20% profit. If he had bought it at 20% less and sold it for ₹10 less, he would have earned 40% profit. Find original CP.

**Solution**

Let original CP = x. Original SP = 1.2x.

New CP = 0.8x. New SP = 1.2x − 10.

$$
1.2x-10=1.4(0.8x)
$$

$$
1.2x-10=1.12x
$$

$$
0.08x=10\Rightarrow x=\boxed{₹125}
$$

**Shortcut — compare percentages of original CP:**

New SP = 140% × 80% = 112% of original CP. Original SP = 120%. Difference = 8% of original CP = ₹10.

$$
CP=\frac{10\times100}{8}=₹125
$$

**Answer: ₹125.**

### Q30. Same selling price, 25% gain and 25% loss

A seller sells two articles at the same selling price. He gains 25% on one and loses 25% on the other. Find overall loss percentage.

**Shortcut — equal SP and equal gain/loss rate:**

$$
\text{Overall loss}\%=\frac{x^2}{100}
=\frac{25^2}{100}=6.25\%
$$

**Traditional verification:** Assume SP of each article = ₹100.

$$
CP_1=\frac{100}{1.25}=₹80
$$

$$
CP_2=\frac{100}{0.75}=₹133.333\ldots
$$

Total CP = ₹213.333… and total SP = ₹200. Therefore, the overall loss is 6.25%.

**Answer: 6.25% loss.**

**Trap:** This shortcut applies because the selling prices are equal. It is not a general formula for equal cost prices.

# Averages

## Concepts

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 6bcf9af71495d346 -->
### Average as equal sharing

The arithmetic average is the sum of the observations divided by their count:

$$
\text{Average}=\frac{\text{Sum of observations}}{\text{Number of observations}}
$$

Rearranging:

$$
\text{Total}=\text{Average}\times\text{Number of observations}
$$

The total-sum method is useful when observations are added to or removed from a group.

> [!abstract] Core idea
> Convert an average into a total, update the total and count, and then calculate the new average.

### Average adjustment

When one value is added to a group, adjust the old average by the difference between the new value and the old average.

**Example:** The average of 8 numbers is 25. A ninth number, 34, is added.

Original total:

$$
8\times25=200
$$

New total:

$$
200+34=234
$$

New average:

$$
\frac{234}{9}=\boxed{26}
$$

**Shortcut — average adjustment**

$$
\boxed{\text{New average}=\text{Old average}+\frac{\text{New value}-\text{Old average}}{\text{New count}}}
$$

$$
25+\frac{34-25}{9}=\boxed{26}
$$

The denominator is the new group size.

### Deviation method

Instead of adding large values, choose a convenient assumed average and add the deviations from it.

**Example:** Find the average of 48, 52, 55, 60 and 65. Assume 50.

| Number | Deviation from 50 |
|---:|---:|
| 48 | −2 |
| 52 | +2 |
| 55 | +5 |
| 60 | +10 |
| 65 | +15 |
| **Total** | **+30** |

Therefore:

$$
\text{Actual average}=50+\frac{30}{5}=\boxed{56}
$$

**General formula**

$$
\boxed{\text{Actual average}=\text{Assumed average}+\frac{\text{Sum of deviations}}{n}}
$$

Choose an assumed average close to the given values to keep the deviations small.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 6bcf9af71495d346 -->

## Average adjustment

When one value is added to a group, adjust the old average by the difference between the new value and the old average.

**Example:** The average of 8 numbers is 25. A ninth number, 34, is added.

Original total: $$8\\times25=200$$

New total: $$200+34=234$$

New average: $$234/9=\\boxed{26}$$

**Shortcut — average adjustment**

$$\\boxed{\\text{New average}=\\text{Old average}+\\frac{\\text{New value}-\\text{Old average}}{\\text{New count}}}$$

$$25+\\frac{34-25}{9}=\\boxed{26}$$

The denominator is the new group size.

## Deviation method

Choose a convenient assumed average, then add the deviations from it.

**Example:** Find the average of 48, 52, 55, 60 and 65. Assume 50.

| Number | Deviation from 50 |
|---:|---:|
| 48 | −2 |
| 52 | +2 |
| 55 | +5 |
| 60 | +10 |
| 65 | +15 |
| **Total** | **+30** |

$$\\text{Actual average}=50+\\frac{30}{5}=\\boxed{56}$$

**General formula**

$$\\boxed{\\text{Actual average}=\\text{Assumed average}+\\frac{\\text{Sum of deviations}}{n}}$$

Choose an assumed average close to the given values to keep deviations small.

## Alligation — the cross method

Alligation finds the mixing ratio of two components when their values and the desired mean are known.

**Example:** Rice costing ₹40/kg and ₹60/kg is mixed to obtain a mixture worth ₹45/kg.

Traditional equation, with quantities x and y:

$$\\frac{40x+60y}{x+y}=45$$

$$40x+60y=45x+45y$$

$$15y=5x\\Rightarrow x:y=3:1$$

**Shortcut — cross differences**

$$\\boxed{\\text{Cheaper : Dearer}=(\\text{Dearer}-\\text{Mean}):(\\text{Mean}-\\text{Cheaper})}$$

$$=(60-45):(45-40)=15:5=\\boxed{3:1}$$

Use alligation for two components with different prices, concentrations or averages. The target mean must lie between the two component values for a positive mixing ratio. Do not use the simple cross method blindly when there are additional losses, reactions, non-additive quantities, multiple stages or more than two components.

## Dilution — constant-solute method

When water is added to an alcohol or salt solution, the amount of solute remains constant, assuming no spillage or reaction.

**Example:** A 40-litre solution contains 25% alcohol. How much water must be added to reduce the concentration to 20%?

Initial alcohol:

$$40\\times\\frac{25}{100}=10\\text{ L}$$

At 20% concentration, 10 L must be 20% of the final volume:

$$\\text{Final volume}=\\frac{10}{0.20}=50\\text{ L}$$

Water added:

$$50-40=\\boxed{10\\text{ L}}$$

**Shortcut:** Find the solute quantity first, keep it unchanged, calculate the final total from the required concentration, then subtract the initial volume.

## Repeated replacement

If a container initially holds a pure liquid, and a fixed volume is removed and replaced with another liquid, the original liquid's fraction is multiplied by the same retention factor at every operation.

$$\\boxed{\\text{Original liquid remaining}=V\\left(1-\\frac{x}{V}\\right)^n}$$

where V is the container volume, x is the volume removed and replaced each time, and n is the number of operations.

The formula assumes thorough mixing before each removal and that the container is restored to volume V after every replacement.

## Average speed

Average speed is always:

$$\\boxed{\\text{Average speed}=\\frac{\\text{Total distance}}{\\text{Total time}}}$$

It is not automatically the arithmetic mean of the speeds.

### Equal distances

For two equal-distance journeys at speeds u and v:

$$\\boxed{\\text{Average speed}=\\frac{2uv}{u+v}}$$

This is the harmonic mean.

**Example:** A car travels 60 km at 30 km/h and another 60 km at 60 km/h.

$$t_1=60/30=2\\text{ h},\\qquad t_2=60/60=1\\text{ h}$$

$$\\text{Average speed}=120/(2+1)=\\boxed{40\\text{ km/h}}$$

### Equal times

If a vehicle travels for equal amounts of time at speeds u and v:

$$\\boxed{\\text{Average speed}=\\frac{u+v}{2}}$$

This is the arithmetic mean. Identify whether distance or time is equal before choosing a shortcut.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 9166c0bc7c561b93 -->

## Formulas / rules

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 36f5eb381c077685 -->
### Core average formulas

$$
\text{Average}=\frac{\text{Total}}{\text{Number of observations}}
$$

$$
\text{Total}=\text{Average}\times\text{Number of observations}
$$

### When a new observation joins

If n observations have average A and a new value x joins:

$$
\text{New average}=\frac{nA+x}{n+1}
$$

Equivalent adjustment form:

$$
\boxed{\text{New average}=A+\frac{x-A}{n+1}}
$$

If the average remains unchanged:

$$
\frac{nA+x}{n+1}=A\Rightarrow x=A
$$

Thus, if one new observation joins without changing the average, that observation must equal the old average.

### Deviation formula

$$
\boxed{\text{Actual average}=\text{Assumed average}+\frac{\sum \text{deviations}}{n}}
$$
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 36f5eb381c077685 -->

## Quick formula sheet

| Situation | Formula |
|---|---|
| Average | Total of observations ÷ number of observations |
| Total | Average × number of observations |
| Add x to n observations with old average A | New average = A + (x − A)/(n + 1) |
| Deviation method | Actual average = assumed average + (sum of deviations ÷ n) |
| Alligation, cheaper : dearer | (Dearer − mean) : (Mean − cheaper) |
| Dilution | Solute quantity remains constant |
| Repeated replacement | Original liquid remaining = V(1 − x/V)^n |
| Equal-distance average speed | 2uv/(u + v) |
| Equal-time average speed | (u + v)/2 |

**CAT decision rule:** Identify what remains constant—total, deviation balance, solute quantity, original-liquid fraction, distance or time. The appropriate shortcut usually follows from that invariant.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: b458c53b75f456a7 -->

## Worked examples

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: efa9792632e7d6ed -->
### Example 1 — Average adjustment

The average of 8 numbers is 25. If one more number, 34, is added, find the new average.

**Traditional method**

Original total:

$$
8\times25=200
$$

New total:

$$
200+34=234
$$

New average:

$$
\frac{234}{9}=\boxed{26}
$$

**Shortcut**

$$
25+\frac{34-25}{9}=\boxed{26}
$$

### Example 2 — Average remains unchanged

The average of 10 students is 60. A new student joins without changing the average. Find the new student's marks.

**Traditional method**

Original total:

$$
10\times60=600
$$

New total for 11 students at the same average:

$$
11\times60=660
$$

New student's marks:

$$
660-600=\boxed{60}
$$

**Shortcut:** If adding one value leaves the average unchanged, the added value must equal the old average.

### Example 3 — Deviation method

Find the average of 48, 52, 55, 60 and 65.

Assume 50. The deviations are −2, +2, +5, +10 and +15. Their sum is +30.

$$
\text{Average}=50+\frac{30}{5}=\boxed{56}
$$
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: efa9792632e7d6ed -->

## Worked examples — mixture and average-speed applications

### Adding water to a solution

A 40-litre solution contains 25% alcohol. Find the water required to make it 20%.

$$\\text{Alcohol}=40\\times0.25=10\\text{ L}$$

$$\\text{Final volume}=10/0.20=50\\text{ L}$$

$$\\text{Water added}=50-40=\\boxed{10\\text{ L}}$$

**Shortcut insight:** Water changes total volume and concentration, but not the amount of alcohol.

### Equal-distance versus equal-time journeys

For equal distances, more time is spent at the lower speed, so use the harmonic mean. For equal times, more distance is covered at the higher speed, so use the arithmetic mean. Always identify the condition before applying a formula.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 301904aeb5f0f651 -->

## Common traps

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: f8ce93ac22eca3af -->
- **Do not confuse average with total.** A change in the average does not directly tell you the change in the total unless the group size is known.
- **Update the count.** When one observation joins n existing observations, the new count is n + 1.
- **Use the new group size** in the average-adjustment shortcut.
- **Deviation signs matter.** Values below the assumed average have negative deviations; values above it have positive deviations.
- **Average unchanged does not mean total unchanged.** If one observation joins, the total rises by exactly the old average.
- **Choose a convenient assumed average** to keep deviations small and calculations quick.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: f8ce93ac22eca3af -->

## Common CAT traps

- **Wrong denominator in average adjustment:** after adding one observation, divide the revised total by n + 1.
- **Deviation signs:** values below the assumed average have negative deviations; values above it have positive deviations.
- **Alligation order:** cross-differences give the opposite component's quantity. Cheaper quantity is paired with (dearer − mean).
- **Alligation validity:** for a positive two-component mixture, the target mean must lie between the component values.
- **Dilution:** adding water does not change the amount of alcohol or salt already present.
- **Repeated replacement:** every removal takes out some of the original liquid and some replacement liquid. Do not subtract x litres of original liquid each round.
- **Mixing assumption:** repeated-replacement formula requires thorough mixing before each removal.
- **Average speed:** use total distance ÷ total time. Equal distances call for the harmonic mean; equal times call for the arithmetic mean.
- **Units:** keep distance, time, speed, volume and concentration units consistent.
- **Salt added to solution:** aptitude questions may assume additive quantities. In a physical mixture, salt is measured by mass and density/volume effects may matter; follow the question's intended convention.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 5b5d7846f8caa02e -->

## Practice and mistakes

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: fd9f373d14987dff -->
- [ ] I can convert an average into a total.
- [ ] I update the observation count when a value joins or leaves.
- [ ] I can use the average-adjustment shortcut.
- [ ] I can identify the new value when the average remains unchanged.
- [ ] I can use positive and negative deviations correctly.

## CAT practice — detailed solutions and shortcuts

### Question 23 — Repeated replacement

**Question:** A 100-litre container contains milk. Twenty litres are removed and replaced with water. This process is repeated three times. Find the quantity of milk remaining.

**Step 1: Fraction retained in one operation**

$$1-\\frac{20}{100}=\\frac45$$

**Step 2: Apply the retention factor three times**

$$\\text{Milk remaining}=100\\left(\\frac45\\right)^3$$

$$=100\\times\\frac{64}{125}=\\boxed{51.2\\text{ litres}}$$

**Shortcut:** Repeated replacement is multiplication, not repeated subtraction. Multiply the original quantity by the retention fraction raised to the number of operations.

**Answer: 51.2 litres of milk.**

### Question 25 — Average speed over two journeys

**Question:** A car travels 40 km at 40 km/h and another 80 km at 80 km/h. Find its average speed.

**Step 1: Calculate each time**

$$t_1=40/40=1\\text{ hour}$$

$$t_2=80/80=1\\text{ hour}$$

**Step 2: Total distance and time**

$$D=40+80=120\\text{ km},\\qquad T=1+1=2\\text{ hours}$$

**Step 3: Average speed**

$$\\frac{120}{2}=\\boxed{60\\text{ km/h}}$$

**Shortcut:** The durations are equal, so use the arithmetic mean:

$$\\frac{40+80}{2}=\\boxed{60\\text{ km/h}}$$

**Trap:** The distances are unequal, so do not use the equal-distance harmonic-mean formula.

### Question 27 — Alligation

**Question:** A shopkeeper mixes two varieties of tea costing ₹400/kg and ₹600/kg to obtain a mixture worth ₹480/kg. Find the ratio of cheaper tea to dearer tea.

**Traditional method:** Let the quantities be x and y kg.

$$\\frac{400x+600y}{x+y}=480$$

$$400x+600y=480x+480y$$

$$120y=80x\\Rightarrow x:y=3:2$$

**Shortcut — alligation**

$$\\text{Cheaper : Dearer}=(600-480):(480-400)$$

$$=120:80=\\boxed{3:2}$$

**Answer: 3 : 2.**

**Interpretation:** The mean is ₹80 above the cheaper tea price and ₹120 below the dearer price. The cheaper tea must therefore be used in the larger quantity.

### Question 29 — Adding pure salt

**Question:** A vessel contains 80 litres of a 25% salt solution. How much pure salt should be added to make the solution 40% salt?

**Modelling note:** The standard aptitude treatment assumes the added salt quantity and solution quantity are measured on a common additive basis. Strictly, salt is measured by mass, and a physical volume-based problem would need density information. The calculation below follows the usual textbook percentage-mixture convention.

**Step 1: Initial salt quantity**

$$80\\times\\frac{25}{100}=20$$

**Step 2: Let x be the quantity of pure salt added**

The salt quantity becomes 20 + x and the total mixture becomes 80 + x.

$$\\frac{20+x}{80+x}=\\frac{40}{100}$$

**Step 3: Solve**

$$20+x=32+0.4x$$

$$0.6x=12$$

$$x=\\boxed{20}$$

**Answer: 20 units of pure salt under the additive-quantity convention.**

**Shortcut insight:** Added pure salt increases both the salt quantity and the total quantity. Therefore, x must appear in both numerator and denominator. Do not simply calculate 40% of 80.

### Question 30 — Equal halves of a journey

**Question:** A person travels half of a journey at 30 km/h and the other half at 60 km/h. Find the average speed for the entire journey.

**Step 1: Identify the condition**

The distances are equal, not the times. Use the harmonic mean.

**Step 2: Apply the shortcut**

$$\\text{Average speed}=\\frac{2uv}{u+v}$$

$$=\\frac{2\\times30\\times60}{30+60}=\\boxed{40\\text{ km/h}}$$

**Traditional verification:** Assume the total journey is 120 km, so each half is 60 km.

$$t_1=60/30=2\\text{ hours},\\qquad t_2=60/60=1\\text{ hour}$$

$$\\text{Average speed}=120/(2+1)=\\boxed{40\\text{ km/h}}$$

**Answer: 40 km/h.**

**Trap:** Do not use (30 + 60)/2 = 45 km/h. The arithmetic mean applies to equal-time travel, not equal-distance travel.

## Answer key

| Question | Answer |
|---:|---|
| 23 | 51.2 litres of milk |
| 25 | 60 km/h |
| 27 | 3 : 2 |
| 29 | 20 units of pure salt under the additive-quantity convention |
| 30 | 40 km/h |

# Mixtures & Alligation

> [!note] Topic workspace
> Add your concept notes, solved examples, CAT-level practice, shortcuts and mistakes here.

## Concepts

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: d2649d91f0a1d425 -->
### Mixtures and weighted averages

A mixture combines two or more components. If the quantities are measured on a common additive basis, the mixture's value or concentration is a weighted average of the component values.

For two components:

$$
\text{Mean value}=\frac{q_1v_1+q_2v_2}{q_1+q_2}
$$

where q represents quantity and v represents price, concentration or another comparable measure.

### Alligation — the cross method

Alligation is a shortcut for finding the ratio in which two components must be mixed to obtain a target mean.

**Example:** Rice costing ₹40/kg and ₹60/kg is mixed to obtain a mixture worth ₹45/kg.

Traditional equation, with cheaper and dearer quantities x and y:

$$
\frac{40x+60y}{x+y}=45
$$

$$
40x+60y=45x+45y
$$

$$
15y=5x\Rightarrow x:y=3:1
$$

**Shortcut — cross differences**

$$
\boxed{\text{Cheaper : Dearer}=(\text{Dearer}-\text{Mean}):(\text{Mean}-\text{Cheaper})}
$$

$$
=(60-45):(45-40)=15:5=\boxed{3:1}
$$

The cross-differences are paired with the opposite component: the cheaper quantity is paired with (dearer − mean).

Use alligation for two components with different prices, concentrations or averages. For a positive two-component mixture, the target mean must lie between the two component values.

### Dilution — constant-solute method

When water is added to an alcohol or salt solution, the amount of solute remains constant, assuming no spillage or chemical reaction.

**Example:** A 40-litre solution contains 25% alcohol. How much water must be added to reduce the concentration to 20%?

Initial alcohol:

$$
40\times\frac{25}{100}=10\text{ L}
$$

At 20% concentration, 10 L must be 20% of the final volume:

$$
\text{Final volume}=\frac{10}{0.20}=50\text{ L}
$$

Water added:

$$
50-40=\boxed{10\text{ L}}
$$

**Shortcut:** Find the solute quantity, keep it unchanged, calculate the final total from the required concentration, then subtract the initial volume.

### Repeated replacement

If a container initially holds a pure liquid, and a fixed volume is removed and replaced with another liquid, the original liquid's fraction is multiplied by the same retention factor at every operation.

The original liquid remaining after n operations is:

$$
\boxed{V\left(1-\frac{x}{V}\right)^n}
$$

where:
- V = container volume,
- x = volume removed and replaced each time,
- n = number of operations.

This assumes thorough mixing before each removal and that the container is restored to volume V after every replacement.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: d2649d91f0a1d425 -->

## Formulas / rules

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 280e1516fe441ab0 -->
### Formula sheet

| Situation | Formula |
|---|---|
| Two-component mixture mean | (q₁v₁ + q₂v₂)/(q₁ + q₂) |
| Alligation, cheaper : dearer | (Dearer − Mean) : (Mean − Cheaper) |
| Dilution with water | Solute quantity remains constant |
| Final volume after dilution | Solute quantity ÷ required concentration |
| Repeated replacement | V(1 − x/V)ⁿ |

### Adding pure solute

If a solution has initial total quantity M and solute fraction c, and x units of pure solute are added on the same mass/additive basis, then:

$$
\frac{cM+x}{M+x}=r
$$

where r is the required final concentration.

**Important:** Keep units consistent. For a physical salt solution, concentration is normally mass-based. A statement that gives the solution in litres but asks for a mass of solid salt to be added is incomplete unless density or an intended aptitude-test convention is specified.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 280e1516fe441ab0 -->

## Worked examples

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 4686e823b3f08ebc -->
### Example 1 — Rice alligation

Rice costing ₹40/kg and ₹60/kg is mixed to obtain a mixture worth ₹45/kg. Find the ratio of cheaper to dearer rice.

$$
\text{Cheaper : Dearer}=(60-45):(45-40)
$$

$$
=15:5=\boxed{3:1}
$$

### Example 2 — Dilution by adding water

A 40-litre solution contains 25% alcohol. How much water must be added to make it 20% alcohol?

Alcohol quantity remains:

$$
40\times0.25=10\text{ L}
$$

Final volume:

$$
10/0.20=50\text{ L}
$$

Water added:

$$
50-40=\boxed{10\text{ L}}
$$

### Example 3 — Repeated replacement

A 100-litre container contains milk. Twenty litres are removed and replaced with water. This process is repeated three times. Find the milk remaining.

Fraction of milk retained in one operation:

$$
1-\frac{20}{100}=\frac45
$$

After three operations:

$$
100\left(\frac45\right)^3
=100\times\frac{64}{125}
=\boxed{51.2\text{ litres}}
$$

**Shortcut:** Repeated replacement is multiplication, not repeated subtraction. Multiply the original quantity by the retention fraction raised to the number of operations.

### Example 4 — Tea alligation

A shopkeeper mixes tea costing ₹400/kg and ₹600/kg to obtain a mixture worth ₹480/kg. Find the ratio of cheaper to dearer tea.

$$
\text{Cheaper : Dearer}=(600-480):(480-400)
$$

$$
=120:80=\boxed{3:2}
$$

**Interpretation:** The mean is ₹80 above the cheaper tea price and ₹120 below the dearer price. The cheaper tea must therefore be used in the larger quantity.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 4686e823b3f08ebc -->

## Common traps

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 55508df6c4bea73f -->
- **Alligation order:** Cross-differences are paired with the opposite component. Cheaper quantity = dearer − mean.
- **Target mean:** For a positive two-component mixture, the target mean must lie between the component values.
- **Weighted average:** Do not take the simple average unless the component quantities are equal.
- **Dilution:** Adding water changes the total volume and concentration, but not the amount of solute.
- **Repeated replacement:** Each removal takes out some of the original liquid and some replacement liquid. Do not subtract x litres of original liquid on every round.
- **Mixing assumption:** The repeated-replacement formula requires thorough mixing before each removal.
- **Unit consistency:** Do not mix litres and kilograms in one equation without density or a clearly stated exam convention.
- **Chemical reactions or losses:** Simple alligation and dilution shortcuts do not account for reactions, evaporation, spillage or non-additive volume changes.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 55508df6c4bea73f -->

## Practice and mistakes

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 4a60ebb237b6122f -->
### CAT practice — detailed solutions

### Question 23 — Repeated replacement

**Question:** A 100-litre container contains milk. Twenty litres are removed and replaced with water. This process is repeated three times. Find the quantity of milk remaining.

**Step 1: Fraction retained in one operation**

$$
1-\frac{20}{100}=\frac45
$$

**Step 2: Apply the retention factor three times**

$$
\text{Milk remaining}=100\left(\frac45\right)^3
$$

$$
=100\times\frac{64}{125}=\boxed{51.2\text{ litres}}
$$

**Shortcut:** Multiply the original quantity by the retention fraction raised to the number of operations.

**Answer: 51.2 litres of milk.**

### Question 27 — Alligation

**Question:** A shopkeeper mixes two varieties of tea costing ₹400/kg and ₹600/kg to obtain a mixture worth ₹480/kg. Find the ratio of cheaper tea to dearer tea.

**Traditional method:** Let the quantities be x and y kg.

$$
\frac{400x+600y}{x+y}=480
$$

$$
400x+600y=480x+480y
$$

$$
120y=80x\Rightarrow x:y=3:2
$$

**Shortcut — alligation**

$$
\text{Cheaper : Dearer}=(600-480):(480-400)
$$

$$
=120:80=\boxed{3:2}
$$

**Answer: 3 : 2.**

### Question 29 — Adding pure salt

**Question as supplied:** A vessel contains 80 litres of a 25% salt solution. How much pure salt should be added to make the solution 40% salt?

> [!warning] Unit issue in the question
> A litre is a volume unit, while pure salt is normally measured by mass. A physically precise question needs density information or should state the solution and added salt in compatible mass units. The standard CAT-style algebra below assumes the quantities are on a common additive basis.

**Step 1: Initial salt quantity under the intended convention**

$$
80\times\frac{25}{100}=20
$$

**Step 2: Let x be the quantity of pure salt added**

The salt quantity becomes 20 + x and the total mixture becomes 80 + x.

$$
\frac{20+x}{80+x}=\frac{40}{100}
$$

**Step 3: Solve**

$$
20+x=32+0.4x
$$

$$
0.6x=12
$$

$$
x=\boxed{20}
$$

**Answer under the common additive-quantity convention: 20 units.**

For a physically consistent version, state: “A vessel contains 80 kg of a 25% salt solution. How much pure salt by mass must be added to make the mixture 40% salt?” Under that version, the answer is **20 kg**.

## Answer key

| Question | Answer |
|---:|---|
| 23 | 51.2 litres of milk |
| 27 | 3 : 2 |
| 29 | 20 units under the stated additive-quantity convention; 20 kg if the initial solution is 80 kg |

# Percentages

## Practice questions — application of percentages

*The following are original practice questions. Suggested times are intended as pacing targets.*

### Q2. Expenditure unchanged after a price decrease

**Question**

The price of sugar decreases by 20%. By what percentage can a consumer increase consumption so that expenditure remains unchanged?

<text>Suggested time: 75 seconds</text>

**Concept being tested**

When expenditure remains constant:

$$
\text{Price} \times \text{Quantity} = \text{Constant}
$$

A decrease in price must therefore be offset by an increase in quantity.

**Step-by-step solution**

Assume the original price is 100 per unit and the original consumption is 1 unit.

- Original expenditure = 100 × 1 = 100.
- New price after a 20% decrease = 80.
- To keep expenditure at 100, new consumption must be:

$$
\text{New consumption} = \frac{100}{80}=1.25
$$

The consumer can consume 1.25 times the original quantity.

$$
\text{Percentage increase}=(1.25-1)\times100=25\%
$$

> [!success] Final answer
> **25% increase in consumption.**

> [!warning] Common trap
> A 20% decrease in price does not mean consumption can increase by 20%. The increase is calculated on the reduced price.

### Q3. Finding maximum marks from two students' results

**Question**

A student scores 30% marks and fails by 12 marks. Another student scores 40% marks and gets 18 marks more than the passing marks. Find the maximum marks.

<text>Suggested time: 120 seconds</text>

**Concept being tested**

Both students' scores are measured against the same maximum marks and the same passing-mark threshold. The difference between their scores can be found by combining their distances from the passing marks.

**Step-by-step solution**

- The first student is 12 marks below the passing marks.
- The second student is 18 marks above the passing marks.
- Therefore, the difference between their scores is:

$$
12+18=30\text{ marks}
$$

Their percentage scores differ by:

$$
40\%-30\%=10\%
$$

Thus, 10% of the maximum marks equals 30 marks.

$$
\text{Maximum marks}=\frac{30\times100}{10}=300
$$

> [!success] Final answer
> **300 marks.**

> [!tip] CAT approach
> When two scores lie on opposite sides of the same passing threshold, add the shortfall and the excess to obtain the difference between the scores.

### Q4. Reversing a percentage comparison

**Question**

A's income is 20% higher than B's. B's income is what percentage of A's income?

<text>Suggested time: 45 seconds</text>

**Concept being tested**

A percentage comparison depends on its reference base. If A is 20% higher than B, the 20% is calculated on B, not on A.

**Step-by-step solution**

Assume B's income is 100.

Then A's income is:

$$
100\times1.20=120
$$

B's income as a percentage of A's income is:

$$
\frac{100}{120}\times100
=\frac{5}{6}\times100
=83\frac{1}{3}\%
$$

> [!success] Final answer
> **83⅓%.**

> [!warning] Common trap
> Do not say 80%. The 20% increase is based on B's income, whereas the required percentage is based on A's income.

### Q5. Reversing successive population changes

**Question**

The population of a city increases by 25% and then decreases by 20%. If the final population is 60,000, what was the initial population?

<text>Suggested time: 90 seconds</text>

**Concept being tested**

Successive percentage changes must be applied using multipliers. To recover the initial value, divide the final value by the product of the multipliers.

**Step-by-step solution**

The multiplier for a 25% increase is 1.25.

The multiplier for a 20% decrease is 0.80.

Therefore, the overall multiplier is:

$$
1.25\times0.80=1
$$

The final population is exactly equal to the initial population.

$$
\text{Initial population}=\frac{60,000}{1}=60,000
$$

> [!success] Final answer
> **60,000.**

> [!tip] CAT shortcut
> A 25% increase followed by a 20% decrease produces no net change because:

$$
1.25\times0.80=1
$$

### Q11. Reverse percentage comparison — salary

**Question**

A's salary is 25% higher than B's salary. By what percentage is B's salary lower than A's?

**Concept being tested**

The percentage increase from B to A is measured on B. The reverse decrease from A to B is measured on A. Since the reference base changes, the reverse percentage is not 25%.

**Step-by-step solution**

Assume B's salary is 100.

A's salary is:

$$
100\times1.25=125
$$

The difference between the salaries is:

$$
125-100=25
$$

The question asks how much lower B is as a percentage of A. Therefore, use A's salary as the denominator:

$$
\frac{125-100}{125}\times100
=\frac{25}{125}\times100
=20\%
$$

> [!success] Final answer
> **B's salary is 20% lower than A's.**

> [!warning] Common trap
> Do not answer 25%. The original increase is based on B, whereas the requested decrease is based on A.

> [!tip] CAT shortcut
> If A is x% more than B, then B is:

$$
\frac{x}{100+x}\times100\%
$$

less than A. For x = 25:

$$
\frac{25}{125}\times100=20\%
$$

---

## Part E. Percentages revision sheet

Use this section for quick daily revision. The formulas below assume the percentage is applied to the stated reference value.

### Core formulas

| Concept | Formula |
|---|---|
| x% of N | xN/100 |
| Percentage change | (Change / Original value) × 100 |
| x% increase | Multiply by (1 + x/100) |
| x% decrease | Multiply by (1 − x/100) |
| Original value after an increase of x% | Final value / (1 + x/100) |
| Original value after a decrease of x% | Final value / (1 − x/100) |

### Successive percentage changes

For two successive changes of a% and b%, take increases as positive and decreases as negative.

$$
\text{Net percentage change}=a+b+\frac{ab}{100}
$$

This formula gives the net change as a percentage of the original value.

For three or more changes, multiplying the individual factors is generally safer:

$$
\text{Final value}
=
\text{Initial value}
\prod_i\left(1+\frac{r_i}{100}\right)
$$

Here, each rᵢ is positive for an increase and negative for a decrease.

### Comparing two quantities

| Given relationship | Reverse relationship |
|---|---|
| A is x% more than B | B is 100x/(100 + x)% less than A |
| A is x% less than B | B is 100x/(100 − x)% more than A |

**Conditions**

- In the second relationship, x must be less than 100 because A is a positive quantity that is less than B.
- The reverse percentage is calculated using the other quantity as its base.
- Do not assume that reversing a percentage change uses the same percentage.

### Quick checks

> [!important] Reference-base rule
> Always identify the quantity on which the percentage is calculated. A percentage is not meaningful without its reference base.

> [!summary] Daily revision
> 1. Convert increases and decreases into multipliers.
> 2. Multiply factors for successive changes.
> 3. Divide by the relevant multiplier to reverse a change.
> 4. For constant expenditure, price × quantity remains unchanged.
> 5. For comparisons such as “A is x% more than B”, keep track of whether the base is A or B.
> 6. Use the two-change shortcut only with signed percentage changes.

# Ratios & Proportions

## Concepts

### Meaning of a ratio

A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind by division. A:B represents A/B. A ratio of 3:2 means that for every 3 equal parts assigned to A, 2 equal parts are assigned to B.

> [!abstract] Core idea
> Convert percentage statements into an equation, then isolate the required ratio in the requested order.

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 68934b2c2c1bdd2d -->
### 1. Assume parts — the universal ratio technique

If A:B = 3:5, assume A = 3x and B = 5x. The common multiplier x converts a ratio into actual quantities.

**Example: Boys and girls**

The ratio of boys to girls is 3:5 and the class has 64 students.

Let boys = 3x and girls = 5x.

$$
3x+5x=64\Rightarrow 8x=64\Rightarrow x=8
$$

Boys = 3 × 8 = 24. Girls = 5 × 8 = 40.

**Shortcut:** Add ratio parts, divide the total by their sum to find one part, then multiply each term by that value.

### 2. Ratio transformations

Suppose A:B = 3:4. A increases by 20%, while B decreases by 25%.

$$
A'=3x\times1.2=3.6x
$$

$$
B'=4x\times0.75=3x
$$

$$
A':B'=3.6:3=\boxed{6:5}
$$

**General shortcut:** If A:B = m:n, A changes by x% and B changes by y%, then:

$$
A':B'=m(100\pm x):n(100\pm y)
$$

Use + for an increase and − for a decrease. Simplify the resulting ratio.

### 3. Compound ratio

Suppose A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5. Make the common term B equal.

$$
A:B=2:3=8:12
$$

$$
B:C=4:5=12:15
$$

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{A:B:C=8:12:15}
$$

**General shortcut:** If A:B = m:n and B:C = p:q, then:

$$
\boxed{A:B:C=mp:np:nq}
$$

### 4. Partnership — ratio applied to business

Partnership questions combine capital and the time for which it is invested.

$$
\boxed{\text{Profit share}\propto\text{Capital}\times\text{Time}}
$$

Calculate capital × investment duration for each partner, then form the ratio of those products.

**Example: Different capital and time**

A invests ₹10,000 for 12 months. B invests ₹15,000 for 8 months.

$$
A=10000\times12=120000
$$

$$
B=15000\times8=120000
$$

Therefore, A:B = 1:1.

| Partner | Capital | Time | Capital × Time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | ₹10,000 | 12 months | 120,000 |
| B | ₹15,000 | 8 months | 120,000 |

**Remember:** If capitals are equal, profit follows the time ratio. If durations are equal, profit follows the capital ratio.

#### Advanced partnership cases

**Example 1: A partner joins late**

A invests ₹20,000 for 12 months. B joins after 4 months with ₹30,000. B invests for only 8 months.

$$
A=20000\times12=240000
$$

$$
B=30000\times8=240000
$$

Profit ratio = 1:1.

**Example 2: Capital changes midway**

A invests ₹10,000 initially and increases it to ₹20,000 after 6 months. B invests ₹15,000 throughout the year.

$$
A=10000\times6+20000\times6=180000
$$

$$
B=15000\times12=180000
$$

Profit ratio = 1:1.

**Example 3: Working partner receives a salary**

A and B invest in the ratio 2:3. A receives ₹5,000 as salary for managing the business. The remaining profit is ₹25,000.

$$
A\text{'s investment share}=25000\times\frac25=₹10,000
$$

$$
B\text{'s investment share}=25000\times\frac35=₹15,000
$$

A's total receipt = ₹10,000 + ₹5,000 = ₹15,000. B receives ₹15,000.

**Important:** Divide the profit remaining after salary/commission according to the capital-time ratio. Add the salary/commission to the working partner's share afterward.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 68934b2c2c1bdd2d -->

## Formulas / rules

### Equality of percentages

If p% of A equals q% of B:

$$
\frac{pA}{100}=\frac{qB}{100}
$$

Therefore pA = qB, and:

$$
A:B=q:p
$$

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 8e301f4451f45b59 -->
### Ratio and partnership formula sheet

**Assume parts**

If A:B = m:n:

$$
A=mx,\qquad B=nx
$$

If A + B = T:

$$
x=\frac{T}{m+n}
$$

If A − B = D:

$$
x=\frac{D}{|m-n|}
$$

**Ratio transformation**

$$
A':B'=m(100\pm x):n(100\pm y)
$$

Use + for increase and − for decrease.

**Compound ratio**

$$
A:B=m:n,\quad B:C=p:q
$$

$$
A:B:C=mp:np:nq
$$

**Partnership**

$$
\text{Profit ratio}=C_1T_1:C_2T_2:\cdots
$$

If capital changes during the year:

$$
\text{Contribution}=\sum(\text{Capital in period}\times\text{Duration})
$$

If a working partner receives salary or commission, divide the residual profit by the capital-time ratio, then add that remuneration to the working partner's share.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 8e301f4451f45b59 -->

## Worked examples

### Q9. Ratio from an equality of percentages

**Question**

30% of A is equal to 45% of B. Find the ratio A:B.

**Solution**

$$
\frac{30}{100}A=\frac{45}{100}B
$$

$$
30A=45B
$$

$$
\frac{A}{B}=\frac{45}{30}=\frac{3}{2}
$$

> [!success] Final answer
> **A:B = 3:2.**

> [!tip] CAT shortcut
> If p% of A = q% of B, then A:B = q:p. The coefficients reverse when isolating A/B.

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: cb6ec0a3e33c864c -->
### Example: Future ages using ratios

The present age ratio of A and B is 2:3. After 5 years, their age ratio becomes 3:4. Find their present ages.

Let present ages be 2x and 3x.

$$
\frac{2x+5}{3x+5}=\frac34
$$

$$
4(2x+5)=3(3x+5)
$$

$$
8x+20=9x+15\Rightarrow x=5
$$

Present ages:

- A = 2 × 5 = 10 years.
- B = 3 × 5 = 15 years.

**Answer: 10 years and 15 years.**

**Shortcut — age difference remains constant:** The initial age difference is 3x − 2x = x. Five years later, the ratio is 3:4, whose difference is one part. That future one-part difference must still equal x. Since A's future age is 2x + 5 = 3x, x = 5.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: cb6ec0a3e33c864c -->

## Common traps

- Do not write A:B = 30:45; cross-multiply when isolating A/B.
- Preserve the requested order: A:B and B:A are reciprocals.
- Simplify the ratio to its lowest whole-number terms.

<!-- CAT-UPDATE-ID: 7325a46b00733d86 -->
### Common traps in ratio, age and partnership questions

- **A ratio is not an actual quantity.** Convert its terms into mx and nx before using totals or differences.
- **Apply percentage changes to the correct term.** An increase in A and a decrease in B require different multipliers.
- **For compound ratios, equalise the common term.** Do not add corresponding terms.
- **Age differences remain constant.** Both ages increase by the same number of years, but their ratio changes.
- **Partnership depends on capital × time**, not capital alone unless all partners invest for the same duration.
- **A late entrant invests for fewer months.** Count the actual investment duration.
- **When capital changes midway, split the timeline into periods** and add the capital-time products.
- **A working partner's salary is separate from investment-based profit division.** Divide residual profit first, then add salary/commission.
<!-- /CAT-UPDATE-ID: 7325a46b00733d86 -->

## Practice and mistakes

- [ ] I can convert percentage equalities into ratios.
- [ ] I preserve the requested order.
- [ ] I verify the ratio in the original equality.

# CAT Study Plan

## Principles
- Prioritise consistency over unrealistic daily targets.
- Practise all three sections throughout preparation.
- Track accuracy, time spent, question selection and error patterns.
- Analyse mocks deeply; taking a mock without analysis has limited value.

## Mock strategy
- Before: decide the purpose of the mock (baseline, strategy test, or exam simulation).
- During: note question selection and time allocation.
- After: classify every missed, guessed and skipped question.
- Follow up: practise the underlying concept and revisit the error after a few days.
